parts.title: Passage 3: What Do Babies Know?
parts.text:
What Do Babies Know?

As Daniel Haworth is settled into a high chair and wheeled behind a black screen, a sudden look of worry furrows his 9-month-old brow. His dark blue eyes dart left and right in search of the familiar reassurance of his mother's face. She calls his name and makes soothing noises, but Daniel senses something unusual is happening. He sucks his fingers for comfort, but, finding no solace, his month crumples, his stiffens, and he lets rip an almighty shriek of distress. This is the usual expression when babies are left alone or abandoned. Mom picks him up, reassures him, and two minutes later, a chortling and alert Daniel retums to the darkened l»oth the screen and submits himself to baby lab, a unit set up in at the University of Manchester in northwest England to investigate how babies think. Watching infants piece life together, seeing their senses. emotions and motor skills take shape, is a source of mystery and endless fascination—at least to parents and developmental psychologists. We can decode their signals of distress or read a million messages into their first smile. But how much do we really know about what's going on behind those wide, innck:ent eyes? How much of their understanding of and response to the world comes preloaded at birth? How much is built from scratch by Such are the questions being explored at baby lab. Though the facility is just 18 months old and has tested only 100 infants, it's already challenging current thinking on what babies know and how they come to know it. Daniel is now engrossed in watching video clips of a red toy train on a circular track. The train disappears into a tunnel and emerges on the Other Side. A hidden device above the screen is tracking Daniel's eyes as they follow the train and measuring the diametre of his pupils 50 times a As the child gets bored—or "habituated", as psychologists call the process— his attention level steadily drops. But it picks up a little whenever some novelty is introduced. The train might green, or it might blue. And sometimes an impossible thing the train into the tunnel one color and comes out another. Variations of like this one, examining infant attention, have been a standard tool of developmental psychology ever since the Swiss pioneer of the field, Jean Piaget, started experimenting on his children in the 1920s. Piaget's work led him to conclude that infants younger than 9 months have no innate knowledge of how the world works or any sense of "object rErrnanence" (that and things still exist even when they're not seen). Instead, babies must gradually construct this knowledge from experience. Piaget's "constructivist" theories were massively influential on lxystwar educators and psychologist, but over the past 20 or so they have been largely set aside by a new generation of "nativist" psychologists

-.56 and cognitive scientists whose more sophisticated led them to theorise that infants arrive already equipped with some knowledge Of the physical world and even rudimentary programming for math and language. Baby lab director Sylvain Sirois has putting these theories through a rigorous set of tests. His so far tend to more Piagetian: "Babies," he Says, "know nothing." What Sirois and his postgraduate assistant Lain Jackson are challenging is the interpretation of a variety of classic experiments in the mid- 1980s in which babies were shown physical events that appeared to violate such basic concepts as gravity, solidity and contiguity. In one such experiment, by University of Illinois psychologist Renee Baillargeon, a hinged appeared to pass right thmugh a Baillargeon and M.I.T's Elizabeth Spelke found that babies as young as 31/2 months would reliably ICK)k longer at the imrossible event than at the normal one. Their conclusion: babies have enough built-in knowledge to that something is wrong. Sirois does not take issue with the way these were conducted. "The meth(kls are correct and replicable," he says, "it's the interpretation that's the problem." In a critical review to published in the forthcoming issue of the European Journal of Developmental Psychologv, he and Jackson pour cold water over recent experiments that claim to have observed innate or precocious social cognition skills in infants. His own experiments indicate that a baby's fascination with physically impossible events merely reflwts a response to stimuli that are novel. Data from the eye tracker and the measurement of the pupils (which widen in to arousal or interest) show that impossible events involving familiar objects are no more interesting than possible events involving novel In other words, when Daniel had seen the red train come out Of the tunnel green a few times, he gets as as when it stays the same color. The mistake of previous says Sirois, has to leap to the conclusim that infants can understand the concept of impossibility from the mere fact that they are able to perceive some novelty in it. "The real explanation is toring," he says. so how do babies bridge the gap knowing squat and drawing triangles—a task Daniel's sister Lois, is happily tackling as she waits for her brother? "Babies have to learn everything, but as Piaget was saying, they start with a few primitive reflexes that get things going," said Sirois. For example, hardwired in the brain is an instinct that draws a baby's eyes to a human face. From brain imaging studies we also know that the brain has some sort of visual buffer that continues to represent objects after they have been removed—a lingering perception rather than conceptual understanding. So when babies encounter novel or unexevents, Sirois explains, "there's a mismatch between the buffer and the information they're getting at that moment. And what you do when you've got a mismatch is you try to clear the buffer. And that takes attention." learning, says Sirois, is essentially the laborious business of resolving mismatches. "The thing is, you can do a lot of it with this wet sticky thing called a brain. It's a fantastic, statistical-learning machine". Daniel, exams ended, picks up a plastic tiger and, chewing thoughtfully upon its heat, smiles as if to agree.
